title: A day of wisdom
hookLine: study or practice? two camps of monks, and one question to ask all day
tomorrow: what does a lute string know about trying hard?

lines: READ THE RECIPE, OR CRACK THE EGGS?
cards: Some people learn a recipe by reading it twice. Others crack the eggs and work it out at the stove. Each side is sure the other is doing it wrong.
In one discourse from the Numerical Discourses, a senior monk named Mahacunda finds the monks split just like that. One group studies and explains the teaching. The other group meditates.
And each group is running the other down.

teach.h: SIDE ONE: STUDY IS THE MAP.
teach.b: Let the first side speak. The ones devoted to the teaching say: without study, you don't know what you're looking for. The words were spoken and remembered so they could guide you.
Sit with no map and you might just be resting. Now the second side.

The meditators say: you can describe the taste of salt all day without tasting it. Wisdom is seeing for yourself, in this breath, not repeating someone else's seeing. Mahacunda doesn't crown a winner.

He tells the students to honor the meditators, who touch the deathless with their own bodies. And he tells the meditators to honor the students, who see deeply into a hard teaching with understanding.
Another discourse, the Recital, names wisdom three ways: what comes from hearing, from thinking it through, and from developing it in practice.
Read together, the two camps look less like rivals and more like stages of one road. Today's practice borrows from the meditators, and it needs no map at all.
One question: what is happening? Not what should be happening. Not what it says about me.

how: Buddhist communities keep both study and meditation: monasteries teach the texts and also hold meditation retreats, and teachers often give students a simple noting question like this one to carry through the day.

games.q: what does “a day of wisdom” mean?
o: reading one wise book from cover to cover
a holiday when Buddhists honor their teachers
asking, plainly, what is really going on right now

games.q: who says what — tap the pairs.
p: each side should honor the other

s: in Buddhism, wisdom only comes from meditation
the Recital names wisdom from hearing, from thinking it through and from practice.
monks in the discourses argued over study versus meditation
Mahacunda found them running each other down, and asked each side to honor the other.
Mahacunda declared the meditators the winners

games.q: a friend swears by meditation apps and says reading Buddhist books is a waste of time. state the other side, the students' side, at its strongest.
o: without the teaching you may not know what to look for; study is the map.
books are better, because meditation is mostly just relaxing.
reading is the real practice; sitting adds nothing at all.
games.why: the students' best case: the teaching guides the practice. Mahacunda asks each side to honor the other, and the Recital names wisdom from hearing, thinking and practice.

practice: Sit still, eyes closed or resting low. Each time something pulls at you, a sound, an itch, a worry, ask silently: what is happening?
Answer in a word or two, itch, worry, traffic, and ask again at least three times before the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: A day of wisdom: one plain question, asked again and again. What is happening, right now?

orig.note: Pali: development, cultivation. Wisdom from practice is bhavana-maya panna.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: what is happening, a question that works in a meeting, a fight or a waiting room. Talk soon.

sources.ref: AN 6.46, Mahacunda Sutta (monks devoted to the teaching and meditators disparaging each other; each should praise the other)
DN 33, Sangiti Sutta (three kinds of wisdom: from hearing, from reflection, from development)
